Legal Hypocrisy: Female Genital Mutilation v Female Genital Cosmetic Surgery
abstract:
Abstract
               This chapter explores the many overlaps between female genital cosmetic surgery (FGCS) and FGM. Whilst both practices involve unnecessary body modification for cultural or aesthetic reasons, there any many distinctions between the practices. Women and professionals attempt to compare and contrast the two practices and they offer their diverse views on the current legal status of FGCS and FGM. This chapter explores the legal position in respect of FGCS and FGM and asks whether there is a legal double standard in permitting FGCS whilst criminalising FGM. In addition, this chapter examines whether the hypocrisy in law could act as a barrier to the end-FGM movement and the criminalisation of FGM. Finally, this chapter concludes by proposing a new solution to resolve existing tensions in law and in practice towards FGCS and FGM.

title: ‘What works?’: effectiveness of interventions to end female genital mutilation/cutting
Criminalising Female Genital Mutilation
abstract:
Abstract
               This chapter explores the evolution of FGM legislation in the UK, which has had a tortured and lengthy history. Whilst the efficacy of the law is contested in a context in which there has only been one conviction, this chapter examines whether the law has had any impact in deterring FGM and preventing the practice. For the first time in history the views of leading figures responsible for introducing anti-FGM laws and enforcing the laws are laid bare. Politicians, police officers, and lawyers speak frankly about their role in introducing anti-FGM laws in the UK. It exposes the ethnocentric tone of anti-FGM laws which perhaps explains the polemic nature of anti-FGM discourse. The chapter draws on the challenges of criminalising a cultural practice by outlining key themes that emerged from four FGM trials which featured widely in the media. Whilst the first conviction for FGM was secured in 2019, does this really signal that the law is eliminating FGM?

Female Genital Mutilation: An Overview
abstract:
Abstract
               The introductory chapter gives an overview of FGM, as a practice both in the UK and internationally. It outlines the heritage and trajectory of anti-FGM laws in the UK. As FGM continues to be performed in the UK, this chapter draws on the existing evidence in respect of the prevalence of the practice. The four types of FGM and the changing dynamics of the practice are explored in detail. The chapter draws on the motivations for FGM which underpin the prevalence of the practice. It concludes with an outline of the diverse interview participants that gave their time and knowledge to participate in the research that has culminated in this ground-breaking book.

title: Women’s Stories of Female Genital Mutilation
abstract:
Abstract
               This chapter outlines women’s experiences of FGM. It includes vivid descriptions of FGM including a girl being held down in a pool of blood and cut. However, women’s attitudes towards FGM are far from homogeneous. This chapter shows the nuanced voices of women, from those that condemn FGM to those that support the practice. The chapter examines the key motivations for performing FGM, which include the control of a girl’s and woman’s sexuality, preservation of a cultural practice, a religious requirement to undergo FGM, and fear of transgressing a social norm. Each motivation is explored through the eyes of women who have been subject to FGM. This chapter provides a unique insight into women’s first-hand experiences and attitudes towards FGM.

A Novel Legal Remedy: Female Genital Mutilation Protection Orders
abstract:
Abstract
               As the criminalisation of FGM has failed to prevent FGM, family law remedies have been used to protect children from the practice. This chapter explores the development of jurisprudence in family law. In particular, it explores care proceedings which involves the interference of the state in the family’s private and family life to protect a girl at risk of FGM and it examines the introduction of female genital mutilation protection orders (FGMPOs) in 2015 which are used to prevent an at-risk girl from being subject to FGM. This chapter reviews a number of published family law judgments concerning FGM, which shows many key themes including how the risk of FGM is assessed, travel restrictions imposed, and the necessity of medical examinations. It also examines the difference in the protection that is offered to a British girl at risk of FGM in contrast to a girl who does not have secure immigration status. The chapter suggests that the current application of the law is discriminatory, as girls without secure immigration status are often afforded less, or second-rate protection from FGM than British children.
